commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether identifying and managing conflicts of interest in AI adoption keeps patient safety ahead of commercial, engagement, or throughput incentives, and no study documents how often such incentives have overridden safety. Support for R012 rests on one state statute, several guidance documents, and a larger set of commentaries.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Most endorsements are commentaries or position statements that use "should" language without reporting outcomes. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion does not supply an estimate of effect, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

Utah HB 452 (2025) requires mental health chatbots to prioritize user mental health and safety over engagement metrics or profit, which makes the practice a legal duty for that product class in one state. The other sources are voluntary guidance, including a multi-society radiology statement calling for ethics codes that block data use for financial gain without patient benefit.

The sources propose mechanisms such as conflict-of-interest disclosure for developers, internal ethics committees overseeing procurement, and incentive policies that do not reward throughput alone. None of the supplied material reports the staffing, cost, or time these mechanisms require, so a health system has no empirical basis for budgeting them.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI procurement and deployment decisions made with and without formal conflict-of-interest processes, such as disclosure requirements or ethics committee review, and that measure downstream safety events, vendor claim accuracy, and whether engagement or throughput targets shifted clinical behavior. Descriptive work is also needed to establish how often commercial incentives have influenced AI adoption decisions in health systems.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems may have fewer staff to run disclosure and ethics review and may depend more on vendor-supplied performance data, so the absence of evidence leaves their specific risks unmeasured.
